Fast and Realistic Reflections Using Screen Space and GPU
Ray Tracing—A Case Study on Rigid and Deformable Body
Simulations
DANIEL VALENTE DE MACEDO, YGOR REBOUÇAS SERPA, and
MARIA ANDRÉIA FORMICO RODRIGUES, Universidade de Fortaleza (UNIFOR)
The realistic representation of light within a computational domain is not a trivial task. Although several ren-
dering approaches exist, the ray tracing technique is highly regarded as robust and realistic; however, its com-
putational cost is still prohibitive for real-time games and other 3D applications. A modern tradeoff is to pair
the ray tracing with the rasterization step, the former being responsible for generating complex lighting inter-
actions, such as reflections, while the latter is used to generate less demanding visual effects, such as diffuse
lighting and shadows. The stated framework has been studied by several authors, but it has not been shown
to work both efficiently and accurately for highly dynamic scenes with deformable geometry. Stepping in this
direction, this work presents a case study whose goal is to generate fast and realistic reflections on rigid and
deformable body simulations using a hybrid approach that brings together the Screen Space technique with
the GPU ray tracing algorithm and their respective main capabilities. The results show that not only realistic
reflections can be generated at interactive rates, but also that the hybrid approach allows to achieve a certain
level of scalability with respect to the number of triangles updated on every frame during the simulations.
CCS Concepts: • Computing methodologies →Ray tracing;
Additional Key Words and Phrases: Fast and realistic reflections, hybrid model, rigid and deformable body
simulations

both algorithms and hardware to synthesize certain visual effects, games are gradually moving
from approximated and/or fake techniques to complete physical simulations of bodies and light.
Accurate rendering is highly dependable on the quality of the rendered reflections. A myriad of
materials, such as metal, water, and glass, are commonplace and require expensive lightning calcu-
lations to be computer generated properly. Traditionally, games would employ approximated/pre-
computed techniques, such as cube maps, while offline applications rely consistently on full-
fledged light simulations, i.e., ray tracing [32]. Game engines (such as, the Unreal Engine) provide
real-time reflection techniques for static and dynamic objects, such as baked environmental maps
and screen space reflections (SSR) [30], respectively. However, the combination of these techniques
can generate many image artifacts (such as extended objects and incorrect projections). In paral-
lel, some researchers [8, 15, 28] have been exploring the power of modern GPUs at real-time ray
tracing.
More recently, modeling reflections in dynamic scenes with rigid and deformable bodies have
attracted increasing attention in computer graphics. Prior to the render step, the dynamic body
simulation provides accurate motion trajectories and correct response to collisions, resulting in a
believable world to be rendered. However, similar to the rendering process, rigid and deformable
body simulations are computationally expensive and difficult to implement. Libraries such as Bullet
Physics engine [11] and NVIDIA PhysX help developers by providing a comprehensive set of
physical simulation routines designed toward real-time use.
Many real-time reflection techniques are limited to handling static objects only, with dynamic
and/or deformable objects being ignored or incurring severe computational costs. Among the tech-
niques able to handle dynamic objects, the SSR approach is notable for being fast. However, it can
only operate when the reflecting and reflected surfaces are visible by the camera, which is often
not the case. Despite some quite promising results presented in Refs [8] and [15] about real-time
pure ray tracing, there are still many computational challenges to be solved toward its mainstream
use. With this in mind, this work steps in the direction of developing a hybrid solution, bridging
the gap between current and future techniques.
More specifically, this work extends our previous work [1], initially developed using the OptiX
library [27], by focusing on reflection synthesis in dynamic scenes with deformable geometry. As
described in Ref. [2], we have developed a combination of the SSR and ray tracing algorithms
using GPUs to compose the complete scene reflections. Our current hybrid solution, unlike the
previous works, has a new ray tracing component, entirely developed with the CUDA platform.
The process is accelerated by a Linear Bounding Volume Hierarchy (LBVH) [18, 20] due to its build
time efficiency. Comparatively, the new testing scenarios created show that the CUDA module is
considerably more efficient than the OptiX one, achieving a much more competitive performance,
particularly, in terms of computational speed. Regarding reflection quality, our reflections still
generate fewer artifacts than previous works. In addition, for higher fidelity, we have employed the
Bullet Library [11] to generate plausible physical motion for both rigid and deformable objects. We
have also compared the pure ray traced, hybrid, and pure SSR resulting images using an objective
quality metric [31]. The results show that it is possible to combine rasterization and ray tracing
for the synthesis of realistic hybrid reflections, at interactive rates, in both rigid and deformable
body simulations. Furthermore, results shown that a certain level of scalability is also possible with
respect to the number of triangles updated every frame, even with multiple reflection bounces.
2
PREVIOUS HYBRID APPROACHES AND OVERVIEW
A few hybrid solutions have been presented combining rasterization and ray tracing to synthetize
the final image. However, each of these solutions has fundamental differences with regard to our
work presented therein.

The pioneering research of Chen and Liu [10] in the hybrid rendering has suggested the use of
the z-buffer map source as an approximation of the primary rays to accelerate the ray tracing.
In the context of static objects, Johnsson [17] describes a solution in which reflections are gen-
erated by combining the SSR with a cube map associated with its faces. A bounding box is used as
a backup mechanism to correct the mistakes done by the SSR algorithm.
Using ray tracing, Widmer et al. [33] proposed a robust acceleration data structure in screen
space, which uses multiple depth layers, as an interesting alternative solution capable of generating
reflections.
Cabeleira [9] described a solution based on deferred rendering pipeline, in which all the primary
rays are calculated using rasterization and the visual effects based on secondary rays are executed
using ray tracing. The solution employs both the CPU and the GPU and combines the results
through rasterization, however, it is also bounded to static scenes only.
Another hybrid solution, proposed by Andrade et al. [6], which also uses a deferred rendering
pipeline similar to the one proposed by Cabeleira, uses a heuristic to select which dynamic objects
should be rendered using ray tracing. The heuristic favors the objects that contribute the most to
the overall visual experience of the user, based on the objects distance to the viewer and to the
center of the field of view. However, it has the drawback of discarding some of the scene objects
from the ray tracing step. Additionally, the authors mention that in their tests, they have used only
simple geometric objects and that frame rates between 21 and 28 were achieved, but only for static
scenes.
Morgan [22] also describes a hybrid approach designed for PowerVR GPUs that employs rasteri-
zation for primary rays and pure ray tracing using the OpenRL API [16] for visual effects generated
via secondary rays.
Very recently, Ganestam and Doggett [12] proposed a GPU solution similar to ours in which ray
tracing is used to compute reflections for objects that are close to the viewer and G-buffers that
store an image-based representation of the scene for objects further from the camera.
With regard to our solution, there are two main differences: (1) our approach always delivers
reflections, while theirs may fail when an object or part of it is occluded on the cube map (some
examples are shown in Figure 1); and (2) in their testing scenarios, no reflections in scenes with
deformable body simulations were presented.

Our solution to the synthesis of reflections is based on a combination of the classic SSR (us-
ing OpenGL) with a ray tracer in GPU (using OptiX [1, 2, 27] and CUDA). Our algorithm is fully
conservative by taking into account all objects regardless of occlusion. During rendering, the SSR
algorithm is adapted to output an image channel with all the pixels it could not generate reflec-
tions for and, following it, the ray tracer is invoked for each of these pixels, filling in the missed
reflections. To compare and illustrate some of the limitations of the previous work and the im-
provements made with our solution, the same 3D scene previously created with Unreal Engine
SSR is generated again, but this time, using our hybrid model, as shown in Figure 2.
Additionally, due to the use of the LBVH acceleration data structure, our solution manages to
cope with the vertices transformations at a certain level of scalability with respect to the number
of triangles of the geometries used in the rigid and deformable body simulations, with an even
enhanced degree of visual realism, at interactive frame rates (i.e., around 30FPS).
3
RAY TRACING REFLECTIONS ON RIGID AND DEFORMABLE BODY
SIMULATIONS—A CASE STUDY
To generate reflections during a set of simulations at acceptable refresh rates (i.e., around 30FPS),
we have developed a hybrid solution from scratch with CUDA and OpenGL. In order to be feasible
for interactive 3D applications, our solution should meet the following requirements.
First, it should be capable of generating dynamic reflections of flat and curved objects (with
concave and convex topologies), whether static or dynamic (rigid or deformable), through a hybrid
rendering solution. In our previous work [2], we have demonstrated that it is possible to generate
these reflections for static objects with simple movements. However, following this, in Ref. [1] we
have shown that similar reflection results could not be obtained for deformable objects. Thus, this
work aims to demonstrate that it is also possible to reach interactive frame rates with deformable
bodies.
Second, the generated reflections must be realistic; that is, they should have a visual result close
to the results generated from offline ray tracers. Thus, the pixels created by the reflections must
be calculated from the secondary rays, also supporting multiple bounces. In particular, algorithms
that use pre-calculated maps are not realistic, since the map is usually generated from a single
point of origin.

Third, our hybrid solution must support multiple dynamic objects during scene simulation. A
well-known problem is that updating data structures across frames is rather costly. Therefore, we
will use a strategy to separate the static objects from the dynamic ones, as well as to update a data
structure accelerator, through a fast algorithm to be executed in parallel only for the dynamic
objects.
Finally, the hardware required to run the algorithm should be accessible, thus, pointing out that
soon we may have more algorithms derived from ray tracing being executed in real time.
4
IMPLEMENTATION
Light reflections for image synthesis within our algorithm are divided into three sequential steps:
(1) the SSR [30], (2) the ray tracing [2], and (3) the final image composition.
Initially, the SSR step efficiently computes all the reflections that can be solved with screen
space information only and outputs an image channel with all the unsolved pixels flagged. In
sequence, the ray tracing step is activated to fill in the blanks of the SSR step. The process consists
of launching a secondary ray out of every remaining pixel to find the reflected surface. The ray
can be derived from image channels for world space position and normal position. Finally, the
third and final step is responsible for composing the two previous steps results into a single image.
Besides juxtaposing the image channels, the algorithm adds a small amount of Gaussian blur [29]
to soften any artifacts that may be present. For comparative purposes, we opted for keeping the
previous OptiX ray tracing backend [1] alongside our new custom CUDA implementation. Figure 3
shows the basic concept of our hybrid reflection algorithm, which also supports multiple bounces.
To accelerate the ray tracing step, an LBVH structure inspired by Ref. [18] was chosen. The
general idea behind this structure is to sort all triangles according to a Morton code space filling
curve [21] and then build the tree bottom-up by merging each two triangles into a node, then each
two nodes into a bigger enclosing one, and so on, recursively up to the root.
The space-filling curve guarantees that triangles spatially close to each other will also be close
by at the hierarchy, thus leading to a good BVH tree. The entire process can be run highly parallel
within the GPU devices and does not depend on any previous data or assumption, thus, it is an
excellent fit for frequent rebuilds. A complete LBVH build is done in three phases: (1) compute the

Morton code of each triangle; (2) sort the triangles list by their Morton code; and (3) build the tree
bottom-up, merging triangles into nodes, and nodes with nodes up to the root.
The LBVH traversal is similar to a generic BVH traversal, i.e., top down using a stack to store
intermediate results. However, reflection queries are only concerned with the first hit of a ray.
With this in mind, the traversal can be rewritten as a bounded search that prunes AABB inter-
sections that spatially begin farther away than a previously known triangle intersection. More
specifically, the search is bounded by a value T, which corresponds to the distance between the
ray origin and the closest triangle hit found so far. The value is initially set to positive infinity and
is updated whenever a closer triangle is found. Given a ray-node test, if positive, its T value can be
computed and checked against our current known solution. If the node has a bigger T, then any
child node/triangle will always lead to an also greater T, thus, a worse solution. To steer the algo-
rithm toward lower T solutions, when pushing the children of a node, the child with the higher T
is pushed onto the node and then evaluated later. Finally, given that a triangle is found, its shading
is computed and fed back to the reflection shading computation, or else, the sky color is used.
The Bullet Physics engine [11] has also been integrated into our hybrid reflection solutions for
the dynamic simulations of rigid and deformable bodies. To ensure data consistency, we relied
on interoperability routines between the CPU simulation, the OpenGL, our CUDA ray tracer, and
the OptiX library [25]. The data pipeline has as little CPU-GPU communication as possible and
counts on OpenGL-CUDA and OpenGL-OptiX communication calls. More in-depth, the data flows
from the Bullet Library to OpenGL structures, then to both CUDA and OptiX ray tracing backends
within the GPU memory. Figure 4 shows a diagram with all composing parts of our hybrid reflec-
tion synthesis algorithm.
5
TESTING SCENARIOS AND RESULTS
In order to verify not only the functional aspects but also the visual realism of the resulting images,
the processing time spent, the frame rates achieved, and the scalability of our solutions, we have
defined three testing scenarios for performance analysis. Additionally, we detail each step of the
CUDA ray tracer module (which includes the processing time spent during the LBVH sorting,
building, and traversal, as well as for the Bullet engine) to identify its critical steps throughout the
simulations.
All the resulting images were captured at resolution of 1280 × 720 pixels and tested under the
Structural Similarity Image Metric (SSIM) [31] to verify their quality, by comparing them to “ideal”

5.1
Scenario 1: Rigid Body Simulations
Our first test consists of a scene similar to the Cornell Box [13] with the addition of a reflective
sphere at its superior left corner. Gradually, colored 3D models of the Stanford Bunny are released
off the top of the scene. The process was repeated six times, using 5 to 30 bunnies by increments
of 5. Each bunny is composed of a triangle mesh of 500 triangles and is configured as a rigid body
bounded by a convex hull.
Some frames of the simulation are shown on the left of Figure 5. Moreover, on its right side, we
precisely show the contribution of the SSR (colored in blue) and the ray tracer (colored in pink) to
the solving of all reflecting pixels. In addition, a complementary animation video illustrating this
simulation is available in Ref. [5].
Table 1 shows the performance of our CUDA and OptiX implementations, respectively high-
lighted in blue and yellow colors. In general, for simulating dynamic rigid bodies, we can see in
the table that our CUDA based solution performs and scales considerably better than the previ-
ous OptiX implementation. Comparatively, the execution time for 30 bunnies using CUDA takes
approximately the same time as it takes to process only 5 bunnies with OptiX.
A breakdown analysis of our CUDA solution with a number of Stanford Bunnies varying from
5 to 30 is also shown in Figure 6. It is clearly observable that the sorting and building of the LBVH
structure are the two most time consuming steps of the entire execution. In return, the acceleration
structure does a good job at keeping the traversal times low. Even increasing the number of bunnies
from 5 to 30 (having 6 times more triangles), only twice is time spent to traverse all the rays and
complete the remaining reflections.

5.2
Scenario 2: Deformable Body Simulations
For the second scenario, we tested our solution on a deformable body simulation using the Bullet
library, with soft objects (Utah Teapots) falling over a reflective floor. Unlike in the simulation of
rigid bodies we presented in the previous test runs, the shape of soft bodies change over time and
so do their reflections. The Utah Teapots fall sequentially in groups of five, composing up to six
rows of teapots. Each teapot geometry model is made up of 574 triangles. As we have done in the
previous scenario test, for this simulation, we have repeated the executions from 5 to 30 teapots
by increments of 5 objects.
On the left side of Figure 8, we show some frames of the 30 teapots simulation and, on the
right one, their respective distributions of rays to the reflection computations between the SSR
(colored in blue) and the ray tracer (colored in pink). In addition, an animated video illustrating
this simulation is available in Ref. [3].
Table 2 shows the performance of our CUDA and OptiX modules for this test run, respectively
highlighted in blue and yellow colors. As expected, the higher scene complexity led to a higher
processing time, in general. We note that, for the CUDA implementation, the first three simula-
tions, i.e., those with 5, 10, and 15 teapots produced timings below the specific 33 milliseconds
threshold (or 30FPS). From the fourth simulation with 20 teapots onward, the timings are slightly
above the 33 milliseconds threshold.
To verify the behavior of each execution step of our ray tracer and of the Bullet pipeline, we

5.3
Scenario 3: Multiple Reflective Spheres in a Rigid Body Simulation
In the third testing scenario, we verified our hybrid CUDA solution for recursive reflections using
three bounces in a scene with dynamic rigid body simulation using Bullet, in which 10 reflective
spheres are falling in the center of the Cornell Box scene. Each sphere has 760 triangles. The left
side of Figure 11 shows some frame samples of the 10 reflective spheres simulation, and the right
one shows their respective distributions of rays between the SSR (colored in blue) and the ray tracer
(colored in pink) to the reflection computations. A complementary animation video illustrating this
simulation is also available in Ref. [4].
Figure 12 shows the performance results for our CUDA reflection solution during animation.
Figure 13 details the processing time spent on each LBVH step and Bullet. As a direct consequence
of generating several extra rays to synthesize the reflections correctly, it is possible to see that
there is a considerable increase in computation time due to the traversal step. However, even so,
it was possible to achieve FPS rates close to 30FPS.

5.4
Final Discussion
As shown in Table 1, our CUDA-based solution performs and scales considerably better than the
previous OptiX implementation, reaching timings inferior or quite close to 33 milliseconds for
the test runs with rigid body simulations. In addition, the timings generated by the OptiX mod-
ule present a sharp growth, unlike the ones achieved by the CUDA module. A similar behavior
is shown in Table 2 for the scene with deformable body simulations. Comparatively, again, the
results obtained by OptiX consistently achieved much higher timings. Multiple bounces were also
simulated with CUDA using 10 reflective spheres producing timings around 33 milliseconds.
Based on these results, it is possible to conclude that our CUDA solution adequately handles
complex dynamic scenes involving a set of rigid bodies (Stanford Bunnies) falling near a reflective
sphere on top of each other, and a set of deformable objects (Utah Teapots) being thrown on a pla-
nar reflective floor, even with multiple reflection bounces. Furthermore, the results show that the
CUDA module is even more efficient than the OptiX one for dynamic scenes containing deformable
objects, achieving a much more competitive performance whenever it is necessary to reconstruct
the LBVH structure at each simulation frame. Actually, the OptiX acceleration structures have not
been shown to be the most suitable and competitive solution for rebuilding the scenes throughout
the simulation, consistently presenting a much lower performance than the one achieved by the
CUDA solution. Most likely, this fact can be due to the abstractions in the OptiX library that may
interfere in some way and may compromise the performance of this library.
5.5
Limitations
Some limitations can also be identified in our work and deserve attention. For example, FPS rates
close to or greater than 30FPS were obtained for dynamic objects in our test runs, primarily in our

still room for optimization of our current solution.
Another limitation that we can highlight is related to the camera framing on the scene. De-
pending on its positioning facing the reflections, it may be that, eventually, only ray tracing is
enabled to generate most of the reflections, which probably might decrease the performance of
our solution.
Finally, the most time-consuming part of our execution, i.e., the LBVH rebuilding, does not
depend on the number of pixels that will be ray traced. This means that whether 1, 10, or a million
pixels require reflections, the cost of this step is the same. Lastly, a few artifacts are generated
during the merging process between the ray traced and SSR reflections in cases where the images
do not match perfectly, as shown in the two areas circled in red in Figure 15.
6
CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
The use of ray tracing in graphical applications at interactive rates is becoming more and more a
reality mainly due to the advances in algorithms, acceleration data structures, and hardware. In

The results show that it is possible to combine rasterization and ray tracing for the synthesis of
realistic hybrid reflections at interactive rates with multiple bounces in both rigid and deformable
body simulations generated with the Bullet library, and that a certain level of scalability is also
possible with respect to the number of triangles updated every frame during the simulations.
However, for scenes with a large number of dynamic objects, the problem is still challenging
due to the high computational costs necessary to update the ray tracer acceleration structure.

the use of multiple bounces can greatly increase the computational cost of the ray tracing process.
As future work, we envision several possible enhancements to our current solution. For example,
it could be worth exploring some heuristics to reduce the cost of the rebuilding and ray tracing
steps. In order to ease the LBVH building and, consequently, the traversal step, another possibility
would be to simplify the geometric mesh of far away objects through a Level-of-Detail (LOD)
technique [21].

Fast and Realistic Reflections Using Screen Space
5:17
Additionally, the static scene geometry could employ different BVH construction algorithms
other than the LBVH, removing the static vertices from the per-frame rebuilding step. Rigid objects
could potentially be traced in local space to avoid having to rebuild their acceleration structures
every frame.
Currently, our solution does not use any kind of culling algorithms in the ray tracing step.
An alternative solution would be, for example, to make a culling based on the ray length of the
reflection. The objects positioned at a certain distance (where the ray length could not reach them)
would have the rebuilding process temporarily disabled and only would be rebuilt again when
necessary. In our implementation, only the G-Buffer rendering process activates visibility culling
algorithms, such as those already in OpenGL: View-Frustrum Culling (VFC) [7, 14] and Back-face
Culling (BFC) [19].
Moreover, in the near future, we plan to develop our hybrid solution using the Vulkan API. A
current limitation of using CUDA and the OptiX library is their dependence on NVIDIA’s hard-
ware. With the option of a Vulkan-based solution, our solution could be executed and optimized
by any hardware platforms with support to it, even by those without a dedicated graphics card.
Finally, we expect hybrid solutions similar to the one presented in this work to become a trend
within the computer graphics community and that ray traced solutions running at interactive
rates, or even in real time, become a reality very soon, either by software, dedicated hardware, or
both.
